content: Oxazolidinone prophylaxis should be continued into adulthood, regardless of whether antiretroviral therapy (ART) is provided. This is a conditional recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. In areas with low prevalence of malaria and bacterial infections, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis may be discontinued for children aged 5 years and older who are clinically stable, virally suppressed on ART for at least 6 months, and have a CD4 count greater than 350 cells/mm³. This is a strong recommendation, though based on very low-quality evidence. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for HIV-exposed infants starting at 4 to 6 weeks of age and should continue until HIV infection is excluded through age-appropriate testing after breastfeeding cessation. This is a strong recommendation supported by very low-quality evidence. For children living with HIV, those without symptoms such as poor weight gain, fever, or cough are unlikely to have active tuberculosis (TB). However, children with these symptoms or a history of contact with a TB case should be evaluated for TB and other conditions. If no TB is found, isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) should be offered regardless of age. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. Children over 12 months of age who are unlikely to have active TB based on symptom screening and have no TB contact should receive 6 months of IPT (10 mg/kg/day) as part of comprehensive HIV care. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. Children and adolescents aged 5–17 years should engage in at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity daily, with additional health benefits from exceeding this duration. Most activity should be aerobic, with vigorous-intensity activities, including muscleand bone-strengthening exercises, incorporated at least three times per week. This is a strong recommendation supported by high-quality evidence. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends reducing free sugar intake throughout life. Adults and children should limit free sugar consumption to less than 10% of total energy intake, with a further reduction to below 5% suggested for additional health benefits. Free sugars include those added to foods and beverages, as well as sugars naturally present in honey, syrups, and fruit juices. These recommendations are based on evidence linking free sugar intake to body weight and dental caries. For children with non-severe pneumonia, oral amoxicillin is recommended as first-line treatment. In areas with low HIV prevalence, amoxicillin should be given at 40 mg/kg per dose twice daily for 3 days. In high HIV prevalence settings, the duration should be extended to 5 days. Children who fail first-line treatment should be referred for second-line therapy. For severe pneumonia, children aged 2–59 months should be treated with oral amoxicillin at 40 mg/kg per dose twice daily for 5 days. For very severe pneumonia, parenteral ampicillin (or penicillin) plus gentamicin is recommended as first-line treatment. Ceftriaxone may be used as a second-line treatment if first-line therapy fails. For acute otitis media, children should be treated with oral amoxicillin at 40 mg/kg twice daily for 7–10 days. If pathogens are known to be sensitive to co-trimoxazole, it may be used as an alternative. For chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM), treatment should include aural toilet and quinolone ear drops three times daily for two weeks. Topical steroids should not be used for CSOM. In cases of suspected malaria, parasitological testing (microscopy or rapid diagnostic tests) should confirm the diagnosis. For uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) are recommended, with a 3-day treatment duration. For severe malaria, intravenous or intramuscular artesunate should be administered for at least 24 hours, followed by a 3-day ACT course once oral therapy is tolerated. Pre-referral treatment for severe malaria includes a single intramuscular dose of artesunate, artemether, or quinine, depending on availability. For tuberculosis (TB) in children, Xpert MTB/RIF is recommended as the initial diagnostic test for pulmonary TB and rifampicin resistance, particularly in cases of suspected multidrug-resistant TB or HIV-associated TB. For treatment, children with pulmonary TB should receive daily doses of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, with specific dosages based on weight. In settings with low HIV prevalence, a 6-month regimen of isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide is recommended. For TB meningitis or osteoarticular TB, a 12-month regimen is advised, starting with 2 months of four drugs followed by 10 months of two drugs. Children with active TB and severe acute malnutrition should be managed according to WHO guidelines for severe malnutrition. Those with moderate undernutrition should receive nutritional assessment, counseling, and locally available nutrient-rich or fortified foods to restore normal nutritional status. For acute bacterial meningitis, empirical treatment with third-generation cephalosporins, such as ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, is recommended.
